rashi:a2.1: And this matter applies: that a vow taken on the consent of the public has no nullification.
rashi:a2.2: Upon whom Rav Aḥa administered a vow: that he would no longer teach children.
rashi:a2.3: He was negligent with the children: he would beat them, and they would die. [So Rashi’s printed text reads; the Gemara itself says only that he hit them too much.]
rashi:a3.1: By acceptance: without a vow. With regard to [forbidden] women, his inclination overpowers him; therefore we administer a vow to him.
rashi:a5.1: MISHNA: There is a firstborn for inheritance: to take a double portion.
rashi:a5.2: For the priest: to give the priest his redemption, five sela’im.
rashi:a6.1: One who comes after nonviable fetuses, even though the head of the nonviable fetus emerged alive: for example, there were twins, one a nonviable fetus [nefel] and the other full-term. The nefel put out its head alive and drew it back, and its brother came ahead of it and was born. This latter child is a firstborn for inheritance, since the first did not cause him to lose it. And although the head it put out counts as a proper birth, why [is he still a firstborn for inheritance]? Because with regard to inheritance it is written “the first of his strength” (Deuteronomy 21:17): one over whom his father’s heart would grieve if he died. Here a nefel came out and put its head out first, and it counts as born, but it is not viable, and his heart does not grieve over it. But with regard to the priest, this later child is exempt, since that matter depends on opening the womb, and the first one opened the womb.
rashi:a6.2: And a nine-month-old whose head emerged dead: and it drew it back, and its brother came out. [The brother] is a firstborn for inheritance, since the first does not count, as [his father’s] heart does not grieve over it; and with regard to the priest, [the first] opened the womb. But if the nine-month-old [put its head out] first while alive, and afterward drew it back and died, the one who comes after it is not a firstborn even for inheritance.
rashi:a6.3: And likewise one who miscarries [a form like] an animal, etc.: they do not count to exempt [the next son] from inheritance, since the heart does not grieve over them; but they do at least open the womb.
rashi:a7.1: Unless it has something of human form: [otherwise] it does not count as opening the womb, and the one who comes after it is a firstborn for the priest too.
rashi:a7.2: A sandal: which has no form of a face.
rashi:a7.3: Or an afterbirth: for there is no afterbirth without a fetus, only [the fetus] dissolved; and so it does count as opening the womb.
rashi:a7.4: Shafir [a gestational sac]: the actual skin of the fetus.
rashi:a7.5: Merukam [in which tissue developed]: what the tissue of a shafir is, is explained in Tractate Niddah, chapter HaMappelet (Niddah 25a).
rashi:a7.6: In pieces: limb by limb, and [most of it] came out, etc.: this counts as opening the womb. But the head of a fetus in pieces does not exempt: if its brother came ahead and emerged before most of the limbs of the dismembered one came out, he too is a firstborn for the priest.
rashi:a8.1: Who had already given birth, etc.: for with regard to inheritance the matter depends on the father, as it is written “the first of his strength” (Deuteronomy 21:17); and with regard to the priest, on opening the womb.
rashi:a8.2: While still a maidservant: even if she was still a maidservant at her first birth and has now been emancipated.
rashi:a8.3: A gentile who converted: and once she came into the hands of Israel she gave birth. He too is a firstborn for inheritance, since this man had no sons; but not for the priest, since he is not the one who opened the womb.
rashi:a9.1: For inheritance and for the priest: for the children born to her while she was a gentile do not exempt [him].
rashi:a10.1: Converted while pregnant: and her husband [converted] with her, and she gave birth. That child is a firstborn for the priest, since he opened the womb within Israel; but not for inheritance, since he was conceived not in sanctity and is not one who inherits [from his father]. And the Merciful One declared the seed of an Egyptian ownerless [that is, a gentile’s paternity does not count], as it is written: “whose issue is like the issue of horses” (Ezekiel 23:20).
rashi:a11.1: She and a priest’s wife: or an Israelite woman giving birth for the first time who gave birth together with a priest’s wife giving birth for the first time, and it is not known which child is the Israelite’s.
rashi:a11.2: Or she and a Levite woman: for the son of a Levite woman too is exempt from the five sela’im, as we said in the first chapter.
rashi:a11.3: Or she and a woman who had already given birth: and it is not known whose son is the firstborn for the priest. And it teaches us a novelty: the husband of the first-time mother is obligated to give five sela’im to the priest, since he has a male son, wherever that son may be; but [the son is] not [a firstborn] for inheritance, since it is not known whose son he is.
rashi:a11.4: And likewise one who did not wait, etc.: he too is a firstborn for the priest, and he must redeem himself; but not for inheritance, since it is not known whom he inherits. And in the Gemara it objects that he is not even [counted as] an ordinary son.
tosafot:a2.1: Ameimar says: The halakha is, even according to the one who says, etc.: In chapter HaSholeaḥ (Gittin 36a) the reading is “The halakha is: even according to the one who says…”, and in Makkot (16a) most books read: “The halakha is: a vow taken in public can be nullified.” And even on our reading, “even according to the one who says a vow taken in public…”, so that he is not coming now to rule about a vow taken in public, one can still infer something: since he needed to rule that a vow on the consent of the public cannot be nullified according to everyone, it follows that he holds a vow taken in public can be nullified. For if it could not be nullified, all the more so one on the consent of the public, and he should have said “even according to the one who says” without the language of a ruling. And although in chapter HaSholeaḥ (Gittin 35b) we conclude, according to Rav Naḥman, that we administer the vow to him in public, which implies that he holds so, and we rule like him in civil law, and the question there was asked about practical law, still it objects after that: “This works out well according to the one who says, etc.”, and that refers not only to the mishna of our chapter cited there but also to Rav Naḥman. And since Rav Aḥa too administered the vow to that teacher of children on the consent of the public, this implies that he holds a vow in public can be nullified; for it is not reasonable to say that he needed “on the consent of the public”, and did not administer the vow in public, only because there was no public gathered before him. And as for Rav Yosef, who said in Arvei Pesaḥim (Pesaḥim 107a), “[I was put under a vow] in public not to drink beer”, implying that he holds a vow in public cannot be nullified: we do not hold so.
tosafot:a2.2: But for a matter of a mitzva it can be nullified: Rabbeinu Tam says: because presumably the public is content [with that]. And Rabbeinu Tam further said: “on the consent of the public” means when he specifies “on the consent of So-and-so and So-and-so”, even not in their presence; but “on the consent of the public” without specifying is nothing. And [a vow] on the consent of an individual, even if he specified him by name, a Sage can release.
tosafot:a5.1: MISHNA: There is a firstborn for inheritance, etc. Which is a firstborn for inheritance, etc.: here [the mishna] takes up first the case it opened with, and sometimes it takes up the case it ended with, as is explained at the beginning of Nedarim (2b).
tosafot:a7.1: One who miscarries a sandal, etc.: In chapter HaMappelet (Niddah 26a) [the Gemara] explains the sandal taught in [Tractate] Bekhorot: for what halakha [is it taught]? For the one who comes after it, etc. And if you ask: what novelty is that? It is taught explicitly here! One may answer: it entered [the Gemara’s] mind that “the one who comes after” in our mishna is the one born from another pregnancy, not the one [born] with the sandal, since [the twin] usually is born before the sandal. That is why it asks “for what halakha?”: let me derive it from the fact that he comes after the child who was with the sandal, as there is no sandal without a child with it. And it explains that it was needed to teach about that very child born with the sandal, since sometimes he comes after the sandal.
tosafot:a7.2: And one that emerges in pieces: Rashi explained that most of the limbs of a fetus in pieces open the womb, but the head of a fetus in pieces does not. And this matter is a dispute of Amoraim in chapter HaMappelet (Niddah 29a), where Rabbi Yoḥanan holds that even in a fetus in pieces the head exempts.
tosafot:a10.1: Converted while pregnant: Rashi explained: and her husband with her, and she gave birth; that child is a firstborn for the priest, since he opened the womb within Israel, but not for inheritance, since he was conceived not in sanctity and is not one who inherits, as the Merciful One declared the seed of an Egyptian ownerless, as it is written: “whose issue is like the issue of horses.” He gave this reason needlessly, for even without it [the child] is not one who inherits, because a convert who has converted is like a newborn child and is not counted as [the son of] his father. [This is so] even though while he was an Egyptian [that is, a gentile] he was counted as his father’s [son] for inheritance, and we do not say that the Merciful One declared his seed ownerless in this respect, since an Egyptian inherits his father by Torah law. Yet in chapter Nose’in Al HaAnusa (Yevamot 98a) we say: what the Rabbis said, that an Egyptian has no father, is not because they are steeped in lewdness and [the father] is not known; for [it teaches about] two twin brothers, who were one drop split in two, and teaches that they are not liable on account of a brother’s wife. Learn from this that the Merciful One declared the seed of an Egyptian ownerless. So the reason “He declared it ownerless” is needed even though they converted, and the reason “like a newborn child” is not enough; and that is puzzling. One may answer: were it not for the reason that He declared his seed ownerless, we would forbid them to marry each other’s wives, lest they come to confuse it with [the case of] Jews; whereas there it implies that there is not even a prohibition, and “they are not liable” is not meant precisely. We would also require ḥalitza, whereas there it teaches that they neither perform ḥalitza nor enter levirate marriage.
gershom:a1.1: Upon whom Rav Aḥa administered a vow: on the consent of the public.
gershom:a2.1: There, with one who marries women by a transgression, say that his inclination overpowers him [toward] marrying her; and if we did not administer a vow to him, he certainly would not divorce [her].
gershom:a4.1: One who comes after nonviable fetuses: eight-month-old ones.
gershom:a5.1: And even though its head emerged alive: since it is not viable, the one who comes after it is a firstborn for inheritance; but he is not a firstborn for the priest, since he is not the one who opened the womb.
gershom:a6.1: And the Rabbis say: [the next son] is always a firstborn for the priest too, unless the miscarried fetus has a human form.
gershom:a8.1: Or she gave birth while still a maidservant, or gave birth while still a gentile, and afterward married a Jew who had no sons: [the son is] a firstborn for inheritance, since he is “the first of his strength.”
gershom:a9.1: Until they open the womb in Israel: that is, the one who comes after is always a firstborn for the priest too, unless they opened the womb of a Jewish woman in Israel; that is, those she bore while a gentile do not count to exempt the one who comes after from [the redemption paid to] the priest.
gershom:a10.1: Or she converted while pregnant, or was emancipated while pregnant: this child is a firstborn for the priest, since he was born in Judaism, and he is obligated to redeem himself.
gershom:a11.1: And this woman who had not given birth: even though she gave birth together with a priest’s wife and their babies were mixed up, or she and a Levite woman, or she and a woman who had already given birth, and it is not known which is the firstborn obligated in redemption, even so he is a firstborn for the priest. And likewise one who did not wait, etc.
rashi:b1.1: GEMARA: The head does not exempt with nonviable fetuses: an eight-month-old that put out its head alive and drew it back, and its brother came ahead of it and was born: [the brother] is a firstborn for the priest, since the head of a nonviable fetus does not exempt him until its head and most [of its body] emerge.
rashi:b2.1: The breath of life in its nostrils: for one that is viable, go by its nostrils, that is, its head. But if it is not viable, its nostrils do not count.
rashi:b3.1: In any event it teaches: a nonviable fetus whose head emerged exempts the one who comes after it from [redemption by] the priest.
rashi:b4.1: Since it needs to teach in the latter clause “a nine-month-old whose head emerged dead”: where it could not teach “most of it” explicitly, even though [the latter clause] itself means only most of it. It could not teach “most of it” in the latter clause because it wants an inference from it: the reason is that its head [emerged] dead, but if its head [emerged] alive, the later son is not a firstborn even for inheritance, since the head of a living nine-month-old is certainly a birth. Had it taught “most of it, dead”, the inference would be only that if most of it [emerged] alive the later son is not a firstborn even for inheritance; it would not be implied that he loses the inheritance if its head emerged alive, whereas we hold that [once] its head [emerged] alive, it is as if born. That is why it taught “its head” in the first clause and in the latter clause, even though the latter clause itself, which teaches “its head, dead”, means only its head and most [of its body].
rashi:b5.1: And what is it teaching us: [that is,] the mishna. Granted, if you say “its head” is meant precisely, it teaches us that the head of nonviable fetuses exempts him, and it taught the latter clause on account of the first clause. But if you say “its head” is not meant precisely, and the head does not exempt with nonviable fetuses, then it teaches us only the inference we drew: the reason is that its head [emerged] dead, but if its head [emerged] alive, [the next son] is not a firstborn even for inheritance; for once a living nine-month-old put out its head, since it is not a nonviable fetus, it is a birth even if it drew it back.
rashi:b5.2: But we already learned it: in chapter Behema HaMaksha (Ḥullin 68a): if a fetus put out its head [while] its mother [was being slaughtered], it is as if born, even if it drew it back, and it is not made permitted by its mother’s slaughter.
rashi:b6.1: An animal has no prozdor [concealed opening]: its womb is not between its thighs, so the head counts as a birth, since it is in the open. But with a woman, whose thighs cover the womb, the head does not count as a birth.
rashi:b8.1: We already learned this too: about a human, in Tractate Niddah: one whose head emerged for the most part counts as born. So even if it drew back and was not born until a hundred days later, it is considered born from the first day, and we count her days of impurity and purity from the first day.
rashi:b8.2: It emerged in its usual manner: excluding where it came out feet first, where it certainly does not count as born until most of it emerges.
rashi:b8.3: A refutation of Shmuel: since the “its head” said of nonviable fetuses in the mishna is certainly meant precisely.
rashi:b9.2: [Exempts] in all cases: it counts as a birth from the emergence of the forehead. And “in all cases” is explained below.
rashi:b9.3: Except for inheritance: the one who comes after him is a firstborn for inheritance, unless the face of the first came out.
rashi:b9.4: As it is written “he shall recognize”: and recognition exists only with the countenance of the face.
rashi:b9.5: Even for inheritance: since the forehead too is a recognition.
rashi:b10.1: A gentile woman does not become impure with the impurity of menstruation, of a zava, or of childbirth.
rashi:b11.1: This is recognition of the face: the one whose face was recognized first is the firstborn for inheritance.
rashi:b11.2: With the nose: and this is difficult for Rabbi Yoḥanan.
rashi:b12.1: One does not testify: to permit his wife to remarry, since perhaps it is not he.
rashi:b12.2: The recognition of their countenance does witness against them: the recognition of the countenance of their face is their testimony; evidently it requires the countenance of the face. And the plain sense of the verse is written about adulterers: the recognition of the children’s faces testifies against the adulterers, since the Holy One, blessed be He, forms the mamzer in the likeness of the adulterer’s face.
rashi:b13.1: At its end: once [the witnesses] had identified him properly, the Sages were lenient at the end of their testimony, to accept them even from a slave or a maidservant.
rashi:b13.2: But at the beginning: the beginning of the testimony, that is, seeing the dead man, they were not lenient, until they recognize him well.
tosafot:b4.1: And since it needs to teach in the latter clause a nine-month-old, etc.: from [the first clause] itself it could have said that it uses “its head” because that implies a nonviable fetus specifically, whereas after a viable one the one who comes after is not a firstborn even for inheritance; but from the latter clause it infers this more simply.
tosafot:b6.1: A human cannot be derived from an animal, since it has no prozdor: the prozdor here, at the beginning of Behema HaMaksha (Ḥullin 68a), and in Shabbat, chapter Amar Rabbi Akiva (86b), are the same, and it is not like the one in chapter Yotzei Dofen (Niddah 42b), [where] once a fetus has put its head out beyond the prozdor it is as if born. For if it were the prozdor of that passage, what could the prozdor here do to hold back the birth, once the head is outside it? Rather, the prozdor there is the outer chamber, while the prozdor here is the thickness of the thighs that cover the womb between them; and I would have said that the head’s leaving the womb does not count as a birth. Nor is it surprising that the term is the same while its meaning is not, for we find the same above in chapter HaLoke’aḥ Behema (Bekhorot 20a): a tinnuf [a shapeless discharge] exempts from firstborn status, since it counts as a fetus, and that is not like the tinnuf in chapter HaMappelet (Niddah 29a), [where it says] most women in labor have a discharge.
tosafot:b8.1: In brief: [1] The Gemara could not have refuted Shmuel from the mishna in Behema HaMaksha (Ḥullin 77a), “an afterbirth that partly emerged is forbidden to eat,” from which the beginning of that chapter (Ḥullin 68a) infers that the emergence of the head is a birth, since the head may be in that part: that applies only to animals and says nothing about humans; the line there “as the sign of a fetus in a woman, so the sign of a fetus in an animal” concerns only the afterbirth as a sign of a fetus. [2] Nor can one object that Ḥullin’s inference fails because a part may be forbidden as a decree on account of most of it (as in Bava Kamma 11a): if the head’s emergence were not a birth, there would be no reason to decree, since a part could never amount to a birth. [3] And if you ask: since Shmuel is refuted, why does chapter HaMappelet (Niddah 26a) say, about the sandal, that a fetus with life in it counts as born once its head emerges, but a sandal not until most of it emerges, when even after dead ones the head exempts? Answer: “life” is not meant precisely but means fit for life, and the phrase follows the line just before it there, contrasting a living fetus that holds back with a sandal that has no life and slips out. Some books read there “a fetus with life, once most of it emerges; a sandal, until all of it emerges”, which may mean most of the head, and some read explicitly “most of the head”. [4] And the passage in HaMappelet (Niddah 29a), “if it emerged in pieces or reversed, [once most of it emerges it is as if born]; in its normal manner, the head exempts; Rabbi Yosei says: once it emerges in its normal manner for life”, is not as Rabbeinu Ḥananel explained, that “for life” means viable, since even with nonviable fetuses the head exempts, as Shmuel is refuted here; rather, as Rashi explained there, “in its normal manner for life” means whole, excluding one in pieces. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:b9.1: What is the reason? “He shall recognize” is written: It is puzzling: in chapter Asara Yuḥasin (Kiddushin 78b) and chapter Yesh Noḥalin (Bava Batra 127b) [the Gemara] strains [to explain], according to the Rabbis who disagree with Rabbi Yehuda, why “he shall recognize” is needed. Let it say it is needed for what we expound here! For even Rabbi Yoḥanan does not disagree [with this exposition]: he says “even for inheritance” only because he holds that the forehead too is a recognition. And [the Gemara] also strains in Yesh Noḥalin, according to Rabbi Meir, who says a person can transfer ownership [of what has not yet come into being], [explaining] that “he shall recognize” comes for property that fell to him while he was dying. One may answer that there [the Gemara] is troubled by the wording “he shall recognize”, which implies that there is power in the father’s recognition.
tosafot:b10.1: To include what the Sages taught: a convert whose child put out its forehead, etc.: And if you ask: what novelty is there in this matter more than in the other matters in which [such a child] counts as born, such as binding his brother’s wife to levirate marriage, exempting from levirate marriage, one who kills him being liable, and the other matters taught in chapter Yotzei Dofen (Niddah 43b)? One may answer that it was needed here to teach us, since it would have entered our minds that although the emergence of the head counts as a birth, the birth of the rest of the body, which came out afterward in sanctity, also counts as a birth, and we would give her days of impurity and days of purity.
tosafot:b12.1: What is the verse? “The recognition of their countenance does witness against them”: Rashi explained that the recognition of the countenance of their face is their testimony; evidently the countenance of the face is also required. And it is puzzling, for in Yevamot (120a) it cites the verse “The recognition of their countenance does witness against them”, implying that there is something in a person by which the face is recognized, and that is the forehead, since the nose is part of the countenance of the face. And there in Yevamot, after this verse, it brings the incident of Abba bar Marta, from whom the Exilarch’s household were trying to collect money: he took wax, stuck it on a rag, put it on his forehead, passed before them, and they did not recognize him.
gershom:b1.1: The head does not exempt with nonviable fetuses: for a nonviable fetus whose months were not complete, even though its head emerged alive, does not exempt the one who comes after it from [redemption by] the priest.
gershom:b2.1: Wherever the breath of the spirit of life is in its nostrils: since it is viable, its head counts to exempt the one who comes after it from [redemption by] the priest.
gershom:b3.1: And what is it teaching us: [with] the latter clause, which teaches “its head”: that since it put out its head, etc.
gershom:b4.1: We learned it: in Behema HaMaksha: if it put out its head, even though it drew it back, it is as if born, and its mother’s slaughter does not make it permitted.
gershom:b5.1: For an animal, since it has no prozdor, as soon as it puts out its head it is as if born. But a woman, since she has a prozdor that holds [the birth] back, say it is not as if born; [so] the latter clause of our mishna teaches us that it is [as if born]. Still, why was the latter clause here needed to teach “its head”? We already learned that most of its head counts as born.
gershom:b6.1: It emerged in its usual manner: its head first.
gershom:b7.1: Once its forehead emerges: evidently [the mishna] did not need the latter clause itself to teach us that its head counts as a birth. Then why does the first clause teach “its head”? Rather, it certainly does not teach it on account of the latter clause, and it does not mean most of it but its actual head, and it teaches that it exempts. Evidently the head exempts with nonviable fetuses, and this is a refutation of Shmuel.
gershom:b8.1: What is the reason: because it is written “he shall recognize… by giving him a double portion,” and with the forehead without the face there is no recognition.
gershom:b9.1: And afterward she converted: before the face and the rest of the body emerged. One does not give her days of impurity, since the emergence of the forehead while she was a gentile counts as the birth, and a gentile woman does not become impure through childbirth.
gershom:b10.1: With the nose: and this is difficult for Rabbi Yoḥanan, who said that the forehead without the nose exempts even for inheritance.
gershom:b11.1: Up to the nose: that is, the forehead alone.
gershom:b12.1: When they were lenient at its end: where they know she is certainly permitted, since they saw that he died.
gershom:b13.1: At the beginning: where they did not see that he died; to testify about him so as to permit her, nothing suffices but the countenance of the face with the nose.
